title_patterns: [ASSET/INDEX] just hit [specific unrounded level] — the highest since [precise historical reference]
I backtested [well-known group or strategy] — here are the numbers
[EVENT] just happened. Here's what the data actually shows
EARNINGS BREAKDOWN: [TICKER], [TICKER] — what the filings say
[N] [asset class] trading below [specific measurable threshold] right now
Why [asset] moved [exact %] in [exact number of days] — mechanically explained
hook_patterns: Lead with the single hardest number in the first 5 seconds, then say what it does and doesn't mean.
State the consensus claim, then immediately say 'here's what the actual data set shows' before any opinion.
Open with the timestamp/date of the event ('at the close today...') to establish this is a report, not a prediction.
Pose the exact question you tested, then reveal you ran the numbers and will show the methodology.
Name the two competing explanations circulating, then say only one survives the data.
packaging_notes: Two duration sweet spots dominate: 7-9 minutes for single-topic data breakdowns, and 15-25 minutes for multi-stock or backtest deep dives. Sub-90-second clips only work for hard news snippets.
Specific unrounded figures and dated comparisons ('highest since before the Great Recession', '+40% in 5 days') outperform vague magnitude words — this is the channel's natural advantage.
Structural framing devices that travel well without hype: 'I backtested X', 'key takeaways from', 'here's why' — all imply verifiable work rather than emotion.
Timeliness beats drama: earnings reports, yield moves and policy hearings drove most outliers. Publishing within 24-48 hours of the data print matters more than title intensity.
Skip collapse/implosion framing and doom thumbnails. Substitute mechanism-oriented titles ('why this moved', 'what the filings say') which capture the same curiosity with credibility intact.
Ticker and named-entity specificity in the title (PLTR, SpaceX, 30-year yield) consistently outperformed generic 'the market' phrasing.
market_patterns.title: outlier pattern extraction

winning_patterns.pattern: Single-actor, single-action headline: a named person or firm plus one concrete completed transaction (bought X shares, sold N times, split one exit into tranches)
winning_patterns.why_it_works: The title is already a complete micro-story, so the hook only has to confirm and expand it rather than set it up. Our highest hook holds (1.27-1.33) and deepest average views (91-98%) all sit in this shape.
winning_patterns.evidence: The two best-retaining videos in the set are both named-insider single-transaction framings; both exceed 1.25 hook hold despite low view counts.
winning_patterns.how_to_apply: Lead with the actor and the verb. One transaction per video. Do not stack a second storyline into the title.

winning_patterns.pattern: Price move plus an unresolved qualifier — a percentage or dollar figure followed by a clause that undercuts or complicates it
winning_patterns.why_it_works: The number creates the payoff expectation and the qualifier creates the open question. Viewers stay to find out which side wins. This shape clusters in the 70-85% avg view band.
winning_patterns.evidence: Move-plus-caveat titles (a large percent gain qualified by 'catalyst already scheduled', 'headline it didn't write', 'flat revenue') land 67-85% avg view with hook holds above 1.02.
winning_patterns.how_to_apply: Structure as [magnitude] + [but the mechanism is questionable]. Resolve the qualifier explicitly in the first 15 seconds so the promise is honored early.

winning_patterns.pattern: Exact, unrounded dollar figures used as the lead element
winning_patterns.why_it_works: Precise numbers ($385M, $705M, $43.6M, $11.8M, $90.98) read as sourced filings rather than clickbait, which matches our no-hype positioning. These consistently hold above 1.0 in the hook window.
winning_patterns.evidence: Dollar-lead titles average roughly 70-78% avg view pct with hook holds 1.05-1.14, above the channel mid-point.
winning_patterns.how_to_apply: Keep decimals and odd digits. Avoid rounding to 'nearly $400 million'. Say the figure out loud in the first sentence of the hook.

winning_patterns.why_it_works: Every video in the top half of retention is short-form and covers exactly one filing or one ticker. Depth of view collapses the moment the video tries to cover a session broadly.
winning_patterns.evidence: The single long-form recap in the set holds only 22.5% avg view and 0.43 in the hook window — by far the worst structural outlier, despite mid-pack views.
winning_patterns.how_to_apply: Default to short-form single-subject. If a broad recap is needed, cut it into separate single-subject shorts rather than one multi-topic long video.

losing_patterns.pattern: Multi-topic session-recap titles that chain a date, an outlier mover and an index direction together
losing_patterns.why_it_hurts: Three competing promises in one title means no single payoff to deliver in the hook, so the opening reads as an agenda rather than a story. This produced the lowest hook hold in the set.
losing_patterns.evidence: The only date-plus-two-storylines recap scored 0.43 hook hold and 22.5% avg view — roughly a third of channel norm.
losing_patterns.fix: One subject per title. Drop the date. Drop the index status unless the index IS the story.

losing_patterns.pattern: Anonymous-role titles that withhold the identity and the number ('the CEO', 'the CEO already owned X%')
losing_patterns.why_it_hurts: Without a name or a hard figure, the title promises intrigue our audience doesn't trust. Viewers arrive expecting data and leave when the hook opens with setup instead of a fact.
losing_patterns.evidence: Unnamed-CEO framings landed 36-40% avg view with hook holds 0.75-0.81, versus 70-98% for named-actor equivalents.

losing_patterns.pattern: Analytical-verdict titles where the conclusion is stated up front ('the upside is capped', 'is buying X')
losing_patterns.why_it_hurts: If the title delivers the judgment, there is no reason to watch for it. Retention drops to the 40% band even when the topic is legitimately interesting.
losing_patterns.evidence: Verdict-first M&A framings cluster around 40% avg view and sub-0.80 hook hold.

losing_patterns.why_it_hurts: The colon splits the title into a label and a fragment, so neither half is a complete claim. Both instances in the set underperformed on depth of view.
losing_patterns.evidence: Colon-structured ticker titles came in at 40.7% and near-zero measurable retention, well below the channel median.

notes: Sample is thin — 20 videos, all under 120 views — so treat these as directional. The retention signal is far more reliable than the view-count signal; views here mostly reflect distribution noise, not title quality.

The insider_watch franchise is bimodal: named-person, exact-number entries are our best retainers (91-98% avg view), while vague or colon-formatted entries in the same franchise are our worst. The franchise label isn't the driver — title specificity is.

Long-form is currently a structural liability: the only long video in the period retained a third as well as the short-form average. Two entries returned null hook data, so treat their retention readings as unverified rather than confirmed failures.
own_patterns.title: own-channel lessons
